title: Paucamp
summary: Paucamp, also recorded as Paueumpt, was a Corchaug elder associated with the Peconic Bay and Occabauk / Aquebogue landscape. The surviving record is brief but valuable because it preserves Indigenous boundary knowledge in a colonial documentary setting.
content:
Paucamp, also recorded as Paueumpt, was a Corchaug elder associated with the Peconic Bay and Occabauk or Aquebogue landscape. A cited 1660 record described him as about eighty years old, but his exact birth and death dates are not known.

Historical context

North Fork deed research identifies Paueumpt as an elderly Corchaug man, about eighty years old, connected with land near the western end of Peconic Bay. In 1660, his testimony helped clarify local bounds, creeks, meadows, and place relationships. His testimony is one surviving fragment of a much larger Indigenous knowledge system for Corchaug territory.

References

  1. A History of Indian Deeds on the North Fork, 1997, discussion of Paueumpt and Occabauk / Aquebogue boundary testimony.
  2. William Wallace Tooker, Indian Place-Names on Long Island and Islands Adjacent, 1911.
why_this_matters: Paucamp's brief testimony preserves Native knowledge of North Fork boundaries and waterways through a named Corchaug elder. Even short records like this can show how Indigenous people carried detailed geographic knowledge into colonial legal documents.
